AMT original purpose was to prevent 155 millionaires from pay zero income tax.

In 1969, Congress had become concerned that some of the wealthiest taxpayers were avoiding paying any income tax through the excessive use of various dedications. Upon “hearing testimony that 155 taxpayers with adjusted gross incomes (AGI) above $200,000 (about $1,438,698 in 2013 dollars) paid no federal income tax for the 1966 tax year, due to tax preferences or loopholes” Congress enacted the Tax Reform Act of 1969. The Act added §§ 56, 57, and 58 to the Internal Revenue Code. The original purpose of the Act was to prevent high-income taxpayers from paying little or no income tax.

However, the new minimum tax failed to rectify the problem. In an effort to ensure, the AMT met its original purpose Congress has made substantial changes to the AMT numerous times of the past forty-four years. The most recent attempt was by the American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012. The purpose of this act was to prevent the increasing number middle-income families paying the AMT. However, even this most recent attempt will not ensure that high income tax payers will pay federal income tax and still forces many middle-income families to pay the AMT.

In 2009, a family of four making $60,000 paid a higher effective tax rate than 13,500 millionaires.

While the original goal of the AMT was to ensure high-income taxpayers paid federal income tax, it does not accomplish this purpose. In its 2013 report to congress the Tax Payer Advocate Service found that “[t]housands of U.S. taxpayers with incomes of more than $200,000 paid no income tax anywhere in the world in 2010 (the most recent year for which complete data is available), and by one projection about 1,000 millionaires will pay no federal income tax in 2013.”

The AMT hits middle-income families. While high-income taxpayers are less likely to be hit by the AMT, middle-income taxpayers and families are commonly subject to the AMT. The AMT eliminates the dependency exemptions, thus families frequently pay the AMT. The AMT also penalizes middle-income taxpayers with high expenses such legal fees, certain amounts of medical expenses, and employee business expenses because the AMT adds these deductions back into the taxpayer’s income. For the same reason, middle-income taxpayers living in states with high state and local taxes, such as New York, California, Illinois, and Georgia, are more likely to pay AMT.

Further, the AMT adds to an already complex tax code by creating two separate tax systems. Due to the complexity of the AMT, taxpayers filing Form 6251, Alternative Minimum Tax–Individuals, spent nearly double the time on their returns than those who did not. Many taxpayers do not realize they may be subject to the AMT until preparing their returns. Causing some taxpayers, unexpectedly, paying the AMT. These taxpayers may not be able to afford to pay the tax and will forgo compliance. Others must put off certain expenditures that they thought they would have been able to make under the regular tax system.

President Obama, in his budget proposal for the 2013 fiscal year, proposed the Buffett Rule should replace the AMT. The Buffett Rule, as proposed by the President, would ensure “that no household making more than $1 million annually [would] pay a smaller share of its income taxes than middle-class families pay.” The Buffett rule accomplish the original purpose of the AMT by preventing high-income taxpayers from paying little or no federal income tax. The Buffett rule solves the problem that the numerous amendments to the AMT failed to do. Further, by replacing the AMT with the Buffet Rule Congress will free middle-income taxpayers from paying the AMT and effectively decreasing their possible tax burden. In the Presidents most recent budget proposal, he has again called for the adoption of the Buffett Rule.

In President Obama’s 2014 budget upper-income revenue proposals for deficit reduction, including the Buffett Rule totaled 37.1 billion in revenue. TAS projects that the AMT will only bring in $25.6 billion in 2013. This figure does not include a likely decline in voluntary compliance due to the complexity and unpredictability of the tax, thus increasing the IRS compliance costs.
Why we need to replace the AMT with the Buffet rule.
